topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: This research challenges the assumption that maximizing predictive diversity is universally beneficial for deep ensembles by demonstrating that constructing ensembles along the Pareto-optimal frontier of member accuracy and UQ-aware diversity yields superior uncertainty quantification efficiency—better calibration and likelihood per unit of computation.

BACKGROUND: Deep ensembles are the gold standard for uncertainty quantification (UQ) in neural networks, but their scaling cost is prohibitive. The prevailing strategy to improve UQ is to maximize diversity among members, yet this untested assumption neglects the essential role of individual model accuracy and may harm computational efficiency. An open problem is how to optimally select ensemble members to achieve the best UQ performance for a fixed computational budget.

APPROACH: We will train a population of models with controlled variations (initialization, label noise) and define a novel, UQ-aware diversity metric—the reduction in ensemble Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) compared to the average member NLL. We will then construct ensembles by selecting members that lie on the Pareto frontier between individual accuracy and this NLL-diversity, directly linking the construction objective to the target UQ metric.

EXPERIMENT: Using CIFAR-10/10-C, we will compare the UQ performance (NLL, Expected Calibration Error) and computational cost (parameters, latency) of our Pareto-optimal ensembles against standard Max-Diversity and Max-Accuracy baselines of equal size, falsifying the hypothesis if our ensembles do not outperform both baselines on these metrics.

NOVELTY: This work moves beyond promoting diversity as an unqualified good by rigorously establishing and exploiting an accuracy-diversity trade-off for UQ efficiency, introducing a UQ-aware diversity metric for ensemble construction that directly targets calibration and likelihood improvement.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty can be decomposed within a single neural network by attributing variance from training stochasticity (via a small multi-seed ensemble) to epistemic uncertainty and variance from architectural stochasticity (via MC Dropout) to aleatoric uncertainty, validated by a causal Stochasticity Intervention Test.

BACKGROUND: Current methods for uncertainty decomposition, like deep ensembles or Bayesian neural networks, are computationally expensive. A key open problem is whether a single model's behavior under different stochasticity sources can provide a cheaper, post-hoc decomposition, but this requires rigorously establishing a causal link between the source of stochasticity and the type of uncertainty it reveals.

APPROACH: We will measure two variance signatures: 1) *Ensemble Variance* across a few models trained from different random seeds (capturing training stochasticity), and 2) *MC Dropout Variance* across stochastic forward passes of a single model. We will correlate each with established uncertainty proxies and, crucially, perform a Stochasticity Intervention Test by fine-tuning on OOD samples to directly manipulate epistemic uncertainty and observe the predicted selective change in the Ensemble Variance signature.

EXPERIMENT: Using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 (ID) and SVHN (OOD), we will compute rank correlations between each variance signature and proxies (feature-space distance for epistemic, predictive entropy on high-entropy ID samples for aleatoric), followed by the intervention test measuring signature changes before and after fine-tuning.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlative observations by mechanistically attributing distinct uncertainty types to specific stochasticity origins within a single model framework and providing causal validation via targeted intervention, enabling a novel, post-hoc decomposition method without large ensembles.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: This research introduces an orchestrated diversity protocol for deep ensembles, which synthesizes complementary diversity mechanisms informed by a controlled ablation study, to produce ensembles that Pareto-dominate standard deep ensembles in uncertainty quality per fixed computational budget.

BACKGROUND: The field of uncertainty quantification in deep learning relies on the untested assumption that random initialization provides near-optimal diversity for Deep Ensembles. This leaves a critical gap: whether structured, functionally orthogonal diversity can yield more efficient and higher-performing ensembles has never been rigorously decomposed and tested under a constant compute budget.

APPROACH: We will first perform a controlled, constant-compute ablation on CIFAR-100, comparing ensembles where diversity stems solely from random initialization, bootstrapped data sampling, distinct augmentation policies, or a functional orthogonality loss penalty. The most effective mechanisms will then be synthesized into a single, novel orchestrated diversity training protocol for ensembles.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate all ensembles on CIFAR-100 and its distribution-shifted counterpart (CIFAR-100-C), measuring the Pareto frontier of aggregate uncertainty performance (calibration, OOD detection AUC) versus inference cost, with pairwise prediction error correlation as a key diagnostic. The best protocol will be validated on ImageNet.

NOVELTY: This provides the first rigorous, constant-compute decomposition of ensemble diversity sources, moving beyond ablation to propose a novel, synthesized training protocol whose design is explicitly informed by quantifying the drivers of efficient uncertainty quantification.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose a causal test of the "diversity hypothesis" in deep ensembles by treating diversity as a set of independent, manipulable variables—specifically, the spread in architectural width among members—to establish direct, saturating links to out-of-distribution detection performance, while decoupling its effect from in-distribution calibration.

BACKGROUND: A core, untested assumption in uncertainty quantification (UQ) is that predictive diversity is the primary driver of high-quality uncertainty in deep ensembles. The causal link between specific, measurable diversities and empirical UQ metrics—particularly the differential impact on out-of-distribution (OOD) detection versus in-distribution (ID) calibration—remains unverified, creating a gap in principled ensemble design.

APPROACH: We train ensembles where the primary controllable variable is the variance of a width multiplier across ResNet-20 members. We actively measure three diversity metrics—logit variance, gradient orthogonality, and disagreement rate—on a strategically defined "ambiguity probe set" (the top-k highest entropy ID validation samples). We then plot these manipulated diversity metrics against downstream UQ observables (OOD AUROC, ID ECE) to test for causal, saturating relationships.

EXPERIMENT: Using CIFAR-10 (ID) and SVHN (OOD), we sweep the architectural width spread across ensemble members, measure diversity on the entropy-based probe set, and evaluate OOD AUROC and ID ECE. The hypothesis is falsified if increased diversity does not correlate with improved OOD AUROC or shows a strong continuous benefit for calibration.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlation by using active post-training diversity interventions and a falsifiable, decoupled prediction: diversity selectively and saturably benefits OOD detection, not ID calibration. The novelty is the rigorous causal framework that treats diversity as a set of controllable levers rather than a monolithic goal.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose that optimal uncertainty quantification in deep ensembles requires inducing a targeted form of diversity—disagreement in internal feature representations specifically under distribution shift—and provide a method to directly maximize this property, creating compact ensembles that outperform standard deep ensembles in out-of-distribution detection and calibration per computational unit.

BACKGROUND: Deep ensembles are the gold standard for uncertainty quantification (UQ) but are prohibitively expensive. The field operates on the untested assumption that generic, heuristically-induced diversity (e.g., via random initialization) is sufficient for optimal UQ. This leaves open a critical scientific problem: identifying and efficiently inducing the *specific type* of diversity that is most predictive of robust UQ under distribution shift.

APPROACH: We will train compact ensembles (5 members) where, alongside the standard classification loss, an auxiliary contrastive loss explicitly maximizes the variance of low-dimensional feature projections across members, but *only* when evaluated on a held-out validation set subjected to mild corruptions. This encourages members to develop disjoint feature representations specifically for data beyond the training distribution while preserving consensus on clean, in-distribution examples.

EXPERIMENT: Using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, we will compare our ensemble against controls (diversity via random initialization or bootstrapped data) by measuring: 1) OOD detection AUC on SVHN and CIFAR-10-C, 2) calibration error (ECE) under increasing corruption severity, and 3) a novel, held-out feature diversity metric (Centered Kernel Alignment across multiple layers) to verify the induced representational divergence was not directly optimized for.

NOVELTY: This shifts the objective from ensembling models to "ensembling robust features," by hypothesizing and directly optimizing for a specific, verifiable type of diversity (feature-disagreement-on-shift) that is uniquely valuable for UQ, moving beyond generic heuristic diversity or output-space disagreement.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
**IDEA:** This research will conduct the first controlled experiment to test the hypothesis that the data scaling exponent (α_D) is degraded by the temporal and topical structure of real-world data, by measuring the learning efficiency loss when pre-training language models on globally ordered versus document-shuffled sequences.

**BACKGROUND:** Current neural scaling laws treat data as a homogeneous, i.i.d. token count, an assumption fundamentally violated by the temporal and topical structure of all practical training corpora. This creates a critical gap: it is unknown how this non-i.i.d. structure affects the efficiency of scaling, leading to potentially inaccurate predictions of the compute and data required for model training.

**APPROACH:** We will perform continued pre-training from a fixed Llama 2 7B checkpoint on multiple 50B-token datasets constructed from the same arXiv corpus but with manipulated global sequence order. The key comparison is between a document-shuffled baseline and two structured conditions: chronological order and topical grouping.

**EXPERIMENT:** We will train identically on each sequenced dataset, measuring validation loss on a held-out set at regular intervals. The core test is a direct comparison of final loss values and integrated learning progress, with the hypothesis that structured conditions yield statistically higher final loss than the shuffled baseline after an equal token budget.

**NOVELTY:** This moves beyond vague notions of data "quality" to isolate and quantify the impact of measurable, global sequence structure on scaling efficiency, challenging the foundational i.i.d. assumption of current scaling laws with a controlled, mechanistic experiment.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: This work performs the first controlled, isoFLOP test of the universality of scaling law exponents by measuring whether architecturally distinct models (e.g., Dense Transformer, MoE, SSM) achieve the same loss at equal compute, thereby determining if optimal model-data allocations and scaling exponents are architecture-dependent.

BACKGROUND: A foundational assumption in LLM scaling is that the power-law exponents (α, β) governing loss reduction are universal across architectures, enabling cross-architectural comparisons and compute-optimal projections. This assumption, critical for efficient planning, has never been rigorously tested in a controlled setting where architecture is the sole variable.

APPROACH: For each candidate architecture, we first fit a custom scaling law using cheap, small-scale proxy runs (100M-500M params) with architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning. We then use each fitted law to solve for the optimal (N, D) allocation for a fixed, large compute budget C. Finally, we execute one large training run per architecture at its own predicted optimum.

EXPERIMENT: The core test is a comparison of final validation loss between architectures at isoFLOPs (e.g., C=3e21 FLOPs). All models are trained on an identical, versioned dataset (e.g., OLMo's Dolma v1.7) and tokenizer. A statistically significant difference in achieved loss falsifies universality, with differences in optimal N and D directly implying different underlying exponents.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond measuring scaling for single architectures to directly testing the invariance of scaling fundamentals, isolating architecture via a compute-constant protocol and architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning—a controlled, falsifiable experiment previously absent from the literature.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: We hypothesize that the scaling exponents (α, β) are dynamic functions of a model's internal representational state, and that the intrinsic dimensionality of layer-wise activations serves as a predictive leading indicator for transitions between power-law scaling regimes.

BACKGROUND: The foundational separability assumption (L = f(N) + g(D)) of scaling laws remains untested. Its breakdown likely explains observed "regional" scaling shifts, but current work only describes these shifts retrospectively. The critical open problem is to find a measurable, internal mechanism that predicts when and why these scaling transitions occur.

APPROACH: We will train a suite of Transformer models while tracking the effective rank (intrinsic dimension) of per-layer activations. At regular checkpoints, we will perform state-dependent scaling fits by morphing checkpoints into width/depth variants and measuring their loss after a short continuation, obtaining a time series of α(t) and β(t) conditioned on the current internal state.

EXPERIMENT: We will correlate the time-lagged evolution of activation intrinsic dimensionality against the fitted exponents (α(t), β(t)) across models of varying scales (10M-1B parameters) trained on controlled data subsets (C4, The Pile), with controls for architecture and data distribution.

NOVELTY: This moves from describing static scaling laws to a mechanistic, predictive framework by directly linking the breakdown of separability to a measurable internal state variable, offering a falsifiable hypothesis for forecasting scaling transitions.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: We will test the Mechanistic Scaling Hypothesis: that the discontinuous "emergent abilities" of LLMs correspond to continuous increases in the functional robustness of underlying computational circuits, by combining Chinchilla-optimal scaling laws with causal analysis of synthetic algorithmic tasks.

BACKGROUND: Scaling laws show smooth loss improvement, yet capabilities emerge abruptly. The central open problem is whether this behavioral discontinuity reflects a fundamental mechanistic discontinuity or is an artifact of coarse-grained measurement. Bridging phenomenological scaling and mechanistic interpretability is critical for predicting and understanding model capabilities.

APPROACH: We will train a dense Transformer series (100M to 3B parameters), each to its own Chinchilla-optimal (N, D) point on SlimPajama. We will identify a behavioral emergence threshold on synthetic algorithmic tasks (e.g., modular arithmetic) and then perform causal mediation analysis to measure the robustness (performance drop-off under ablation) of the identified task-specific circuits across model scales.

EXPERIMENT: We will correlate the rate of change in circuit robustness (a continuous mechanistic metric) with model scale (N), testing if the behavioral threshold corresponds to a critical, predictable value of this robustness, while tracking standard scaling observables (validation loss) and behavioral metrics on synthetic and standard (GSM8K) benchmarks.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlating circuit size with emergence to instead quantify the continuous scaling of a circuit's *functional robustness*, directly testing the hypothesis that behavioral discontinuity stems from crossing a mechanistic reliability threshold, not an algorithmic discontinuity.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: This research will systematically test the universality of neural scaling laws by mapping isoFLOP frontiers for dense transformers across data domains of varying intrinsic compressibility (code, web text, synthetic algorithms) to demonstrate that the compute-optimal model-to-data ratio and scaling exponents are functions of a domain's learning complexity.

BACKGROUND: The Chinchilla scaling laws propose a universal compute-optimal frontier (N ∝ D) for dense transformers trained on a mixed web corpus. It remains an open problem whether this frontier and its underlying power-law exponents (α, β) are invariant across fundamentally different data domains and model architectures, a critical assumption for efficient, domain-specific scaling.

APPROACH: We will adopt the isoFLOP profiles methodology, conducting short training runs along fixed compute budgets (C=6ND) for dense models across three domains. We will fit the scaling law L(N,D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β to extrapolated final losses and correlate the exponent α with a domain's pre-measured intrinsic entropy. A secondary architecture experiment will use continued pre-training of fixed-scale open-source dense and MoE models.

EXPERIMENT: For each domain, we will measure its compressed entropy, then run a grid of short trainings (e.g., 1e18-1e20 FLOPs) varying N and D along isoFLOP curves, fitting α and β from validation loss. We will validate by training one model per domain at the predicted optimal N/D for a higher budget.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond observing different loss values to directly test if the fundamental scaling exponents vary with data complexity, aiming to replace a single universal frontier with a predictive family of frontiers parameterized by a quantifiable, domain-intrinsic property.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: We propose a learnable, context-aware regularization policy for federated learning that dynamically sets client-specific hyperparameters by predicting unobservable optimization terms from measurable per-round statistics, jointly optimizing for statistical and system heterogeneity.

BACKGROUND: Current federated learning algorithms treat statistical (non-IID) and system (stragglers) heterogeneity separately, creating a suboptimal trade-off. The core open problem is the lack of a principled, unified method to adapt the training process in real-time to the joint state of a client's data divergence and computational delay.

APPROACH: We derive a decomposed regularization rule, μ = μ_stat * μ_sys, where μ_stat corrects for data drift via a gradient dissimilarity term and μ_sys penalizes staleness. A lightweight meta-model, trained on data from a controlled discovery phase, predicts the critical, unobservable terms (e.g., local loss curvature) from a directly measurable context vector containing update norm, cosine similarity, sample count, and computation time.

EXPERIMENT: We validate the policy using NVIDIA FLARE on CIFAR-10 with controlled Dirichlet(α) label skew and Pareto delays, measuring its multi-objective performance (final accuracy, convergence rounds, communication cost) against tuned static FedProx and SCAFFOLD baselines. Falsification occurs if the policy fails to achieve a statistically superior Pareto frontier across all tested heterogeneity configurations.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond adaptive heuristics by framing joint heterogeneity as a contextual control problem, using a meta-model to learn a principled regularization function from measurable context—a synthesis of optimization theory and data-driven policy learning not seen in prior work.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
**IDEA:** This research will derive and validate a predictive cost model that quantifies the system-accuracy trade-off in federated learning, establishing a falsifiable, bottleneck-dependent decision rule for selecting heterogeneity-robust algorithms based on their operational signatures and the deployment environment's compute/latency profile.

**BACKGROUND:** While algorithms like FedProx and SCAFFOLD mitigate accuracy loss from non-IID client data, their comparative *system efficiency*—the accuracy gained per unit of total resource cost—remains an unquantified trade-off. The critical open problem is a lack of generalizable principles to predict which robustness strategy is most resource-efficient under a specific system bottleneck (e.g., dominant computation vs. dominant network latency), hindering optimal algorithm selection in real-world deployments.

**APPROACH:** We will develop a lightweight, analytical cost model that maps an algorithm's operational signature (per-round computation load, communication volume, and coordination overhead) to its predicted Time-to-Accuracy under a given compute and network constraint profile. This model will be validated and refined through controlled simulations that manipulate local computation (via epochs, model complexity, and synthetic delay) and network latency, measuring the integrated system cost of reaching a target accuracy.

**EXPERIMENT:** Using CIFAR-10 with Dirichlet(α=0.1) label skew across 100 virtual clients, we will test FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and a third algorithm (e.g., FedPAQ) under distinct High-Compute/Low-Latency and Low-Compute/High-Latency regimes. The primary metric is Time-to-Accuracy (or Area Under the Time-Accuracy Curve), with hypothesis falsification contingent on a crossover in the algorithm efficiency ranking between the two system regimes.

**NOVELTY:** This moves beyond pairwise algorithm comparisons to establish a generalizable, predictive principle for system-aware algorithm selection, framed as a testable "crossover" law dictated by the dominant system bottleneck, which is a concretely falsifiable contribution not present in prior work.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: We propose a federated learning aggregation strategy that learns a client contribution matrix to weight updates based on their estimated potential to improve performance on other clients' local distributions, directly optimizing for robust performance across heterogeneous data.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning evaluation and optimization are misdirected by reliance on a centralized IID test set, a fundamental mismatch with the objective of performing well on each client's unique, non-IID data. Current aggregation methods like FedAvg do not explicitly use client-specific performance signals to synthesize a globally beneficial model, creating an addressable gap in both the experimental paradigm and algorithmic design.

APPROACH: Our method, FedWise, shifts from centralized to personalized evaluation. Each client maintains a local validation set. The server estimates a contribution matrix by observing how applying one client's update affects the validation loss of others via controlled, pairwise update synthesis during training. This matrix then weights client updates during global aggregation to maximize collective improvement across all local distributions.

EXPERIMENT: We will simulate 50 clients in Flower on a non-IID CIFAR-10 split (Dirichlet α=0.3) for 500 rounds, comparing FedWise against FedAvg and SCAFFOLD. The primary outcome is the distribution of final local test accuracies; success is defined by a statistically significant increase in its 10th-percentile and a decrease in its variance, without degrading median IID test accuracy by >2%.

NOVELTY: This work introduces a closed-loop system where aggregation is explicitly driven by learned estimates of cross-client knowledge transfer, directly attacking the non-IID problem by optimizing for the true federated objective—performance on all local distributions—rather than a centralized proxy.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: A federated aggregation protocol that estimates client-specific task bias from local training dynamics and uses a synthetic, data-free benchmark to weight updates by their inferred global usefulness, eliminating the need for server-held data.

BACKGROUND: In non-IID federated learning, client updates can be harmful due to overfitting to local skew, but current methods like FedAvg lack a principled, privacy-preserving way to identify and down-weight these biased updates. The open problem is how to dynamically estimate a client's contribution to the global objective using only signals available under strict federated constraints.

APPROACH: The server generates a consistent synthetic benchmark via a lightweight generator. Each client's update is evaluated on this benchmark, and its contribution weight is computed via an interpretable heuristic combining benchmark performance change, local loss trajectory variance (as an overfitting proxy), and update norm. This directly implements bias-aware deconvolution without a complex meta-learner.

EXPERIMENT: Test on CIFAR-10 with Dirichlet(α=0.1) label skew across 100 clients, comparing rounds to 70% global accuracy and the standard deviation of final client accuracies against FedAvg and FedProx. Falsified if the method increases client accuracy variance or reduces global accuracy by >3% absolute.

NOVELTY: It replaces data-dependent anchors with a synthetic benchmark and uses an interpretable, bias-explicit weighting function derived from local dynamics, moving beyond heuristic gradient metrics to a dedicated bias-compensation mechanism without violating FL privacy.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: This research challenges the foundational assumption that a centralized IID test set is the correct optimization target for federated learning with heterogeneous data, proposing that explicitly optimizing for average post-personalization client performance leads to the selection of fundamentally different and more efficient algorithmic strategies under high data skew.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning algorithm design and evaluation are predominantly guided by performance on a centralized, IID server test set. This creates a critical gap: in real-world, highly heterogeneous (non-IID) deployments, the true objective is high performance on each client's unique data distribution, and it is untested whether optimizing for the IID proxy leads to optimal strategies for this true objective.

APPROACH: We will conduct a controlled computational experiment comparing two optimization paradigms under high label skew. We will contrast "central-optimization" algorithms (SCAFFOLD, FedProx) against a "personalization-optimization" algorithm (FedAvg with persistent local fine-tuning), ensuring matched computational budgets. The core method is to measure both standard IID accuracy and the true objective—average accuracy on held-out local client test sets.

EXPERIMENT: Using CIFAR-10 partitioned via Dirichlet (α=0.1 for high skew, α=10.0 for control) across 100 clients, we will run each algorithm for 200 rounds, tracking global IID accuracy and average local accuracy per round over 5 independent seeds to establish statistical significance.

NOVELTY: While the personalization-global trade-off is known, this work systematically demonstrates that the IID test set is a *misleading objective* for algorithm selection under skew, leading to Pareto-suboptimal strategies, and provides a controlled ablation isolating the influence of the optimization target itself.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We establish a causal validation framework for topological data analysis by using persistent homology to identify 1-cycles in whole-brain neural dynamics and then employing phase-specific optogenetic perturbation of algorithmically localized neural ensembles to test the causal necessity of these topological features for behavior.

BACKGROUND: A critical open problem in applying topological methods to high-dimensional data is the inability to move from correlative topological signatures to causal, mechanistic understanding. In neuroscience, persistent homology reveals cyclic structures in neural activity, but it remains untested whether these structures are epiphenomenal or causally necessary for system function.

APPROACH: We integrate persistent homology of neural state space with targeted optogenetic intervention in *C. elegans*. We algorithmically localize significant 1-cycles to specific neural ensembles using topological data analysis (TDA) methods like harmonic representative cycles, then design phase-locked optogenetic inhibition to perturb these ensembles. The causal effect is quantified by applying the same topological analysis to the resulting behavioral output.

EXPERIMENT: We record whole-brain calcium imaging and behavior in freely moving animals, identify a significant 1-cycle in neural state space, and localize it to a minimal neuronal ensemble. We then deliver phase-timed optogenetic inhibition to this ensemble and a control ensemble, measuring the effect via changes in the persistence (birth/death times) of the dominant 1-cycle in the subsequent behavioral posture dynamics.

NOVELTY: This transforms persistent homology from a descriptive tool into a hypothesis-generating engine for causal intervention, creating a closed loop where topology designs the perturbation and topology measures the outcome, a synthesis not previously demonstrated.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose a causal topology framework that uses controlled perturbations to test the functional necessity of topological features in single-cell data, positing that the stability of a feature under perturbation quantifies its mechanistic embeddedness within a regulatory network.

BACKGROUND: Topological data analysis (TDA) can describe the shape of cellular state manifolds (e.g., loops, branches) but cannot distinguish if these features are incidental or mechanistically essential. The critical open problem is moving from descriptive topological patterns to causal, mechanistic interpretations of biological network function.

APPROACH: We combine persistent homology computed on single-cell embeddings with targeted genetic perturbations. We mathematically formalize that a feature's persistence interval should shorten predictably when perturbing genes within its underlying regulatory circuit, transforming topology into a falsifiable causal discovery tool.

EXPERIMENT: Using synchronized *C. elegans* embryos (wild-type, cell-cycle gene knockout, metabolic gene knockout), we perform scRNA-seq, compute density-filtered persistent homology from PHATE embeddings, and statistically test for specific reductions in the dominant 1-cycle's persistence using permutation tests on persistence landscapes.

NOVELTY: This shifts TDA from a descriptive to an interrogative framework; the novel claim is that a topological feature's perturbation-specific deformation is a quantifiable measure of its biological causality, which we formalize beyond empirical correlation.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose a causal validation framework for topological data analysis in biology, where the systematic deformation of specific topological features under targeted molecular perturbations—quantified by a Perturbation-Robustness Score—distinguishes biologically mechanistic structures from technical artifacts.

BACKGROUND: A critical open problem in applying topological methods to high-dimensional biological data is the interpretation gap: persistent features (e.g., loops) are detected but cannot be classified as representing true biological programs or measurement artifacts. Current TDA applications remain descriptive, lacking a principled, experimentally grounded method to assign causal biological meaning to topological signatures.

APPROACH: We will develop a comparative topological pipeline. For each genetic perturbation and a control from a standardized single-cell dataset, we will compute separate topological summaries (persistence diagrams, Mapper graphs). We will then formalize a Perturbation-Robustness Score (PRS) for individual features, defined by the statistical significance of changes in their persistence or graph structure across a panel of targeted versus control perturbations.

EXPERIMENT: Using public Perturb-seq data (e.g., Cancer Dependency Map) for 50+ CRISPR knockouts, we will compute the PRS for features identified in the control. The hypothesis will be confirmed if features linked to a specific pathway show significantly altered PRS only upon knockout of pathway genes, not unrelated controls, validated via statistical tests against a null distribution from control perturbations.

NOVELTY: This transforms topology from a descriptive tool into a generator of testable causal hypotheses by directly using perturbations as topological probes, introducing a rigorous, quantifiable metric (PRS) for the causal interpretation of topological features.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We will establish a causal framework for topological data analysis by integrating persistent homology with lineage-specific genetic perturbations to test the hypothesis that representative cycles of persistent 1D homology are dynamic, mechanistic signatures of cell fate decisions, distinguishable from other cyclic biological processes.

BACKGROUND: A critical open problem in single-cell genomics is moving from observing topological features, like loops in data manifolds, to understanding their causal origins. It remains untested whether such loops mechanistically represent lineage-constrained differentiation trajectories or are confounded by concurrent processes like the cell cycle.

APPROACH: We will first identify candidate 1D loops in a wild-type zebrafish scRNA-seq manifold. We then employ a lineage-restricted genetic perturbation (e.g., Gal4/UAS-driven CRISPR knockout) to disrupt a specific differentiation trajectory and track how the representative cycle of cells reconfigures. We computationally dissect confounding signals by comparing topology before and after regression of cell-cycle scores.

EXPERIMENT: Using scRNA-seq from wild-type and lineage-perturbed embryos, we will compute persistent homology, quantify changes in persistence diagrams via bottleneck distance, and statistically test for coherent fate disruption within the tracked representative cycle against computationally cell-cycle-corrected data.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlative topological inference by providing direct causal evidence linking manifold structure to mechanism, introducing the reconfiguration of representative cycles under perturbation as a novel, dynamic signature of lineage commitment.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose that targeted genetic perturbations rewire the causal topological dynamics of a cell state manifold, a proximal mechanistic event quantifiable as specific alterations in persistent homology vineyards, which precede and predict phenotypic outcomes.

BACKGROUND: Current topological analyses of single-cell data are correlative, describing manifold structure without establishing causality. The critical open problem is to determine if specific topological features are passive descriptors or active, causal mediators in state transitions, and to develop an experimental framework that can isolate topology within a causal chain.

APPROACH: We integrate controlled genetic knockout (CRISPR), a longitudinal time-series design, and a two-stage topological pipeline. First, we use the Mapper algorithm to construct sparse, interpretable graph summaries of single-cell data. Second, we compute persistence vineyards of these graphs using biologically motivated filter functions to track the temporal evolution of topological features like loops across conditions.

EXPERIMENT: Using an EMT model, we will collect scRNA-seq data for wild-type, SNAI1-knockout, and control-knockout cell lines across a TGF-β time series in biological triplicate. We will test if the SNAI1 knockout causes a categorical change (e.g., a split or deletion of a track) in the 1-dimensional homology vineyard of an EMT-progression filter, and if this topological disruption significantly precedes the attenuation of cell motility.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlative topology by formulating and testing a causal hypothesis: that a genetic intervention predictably alters the *temporal pattern* of manifold topology (the vineyard structure), establishing topological dynamics as a measurable, causal layer in high-dimensional biological processes.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
**IDEA:** Develop a resource-optimal active causal discovery framework that uses bootstrap-based edge uncertainty from observational data to select both the target and the type of real-world perturbation experiment (e.g., CRISPR vs. siRNA) from a multi-fidelity menu, maximizing the validation of true causal edges per unit of experimental cost.

**BACKGROUND:** Current causal discovery pipelines produce equivalence classes of plausible graphs from observational data, but translating these into actionable, high-confidence causal hypotheses for complex biological systems is stalled by the high cost of validation experiments. The critical open problem is the lack of a principled method to guide the allocation of limited experimental resources to maximally resolve causal ambiguities.

**APPROACH:** From observational data, generate an ensemble of causal graphs via bootstrap resampling to compute empirical edge confidence. Formalize a cost-aware optimal experimental design that, given a menu of possible perturbation types with associated costs and noise models, recommends the specific target-and-intervention-type pair expected to maximize the reduction in graph entropy per resource unit. Validate by integrating held-out data from large-scale perturbation atlases.

**EXPERIMENT:** Using TCGA RNA-seq as observational data and the LINCS L1000 database as a held-out source of interventional profiles, the falsifiable test is that edges whose confidence shifts decisively after incorporating the results of the actively chosen (target + type) perturbation will show significantly higher precision against curated regulatory databases (e.g., KEGG) than edges resolved by random or correlation-based heuristic selections.

**NOVELTY:** This moves beyond selecting only *which* variable to intervene on by formally integrating a **multi-fidelity experimental design**, optimizing the trade-off between information gain and real-world cost/feasibility of different perturbation modalities within the active learning loop.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Develop a differentiable causal discovery framework that outputs a single causal graph from high-dimensional observational data, with edge-wise confidence scores calibrated via conformal prediction to provide rigorous, finite-sample uncertainty guarantees.

BACKGROUND: Current causal discovery methods output equivalence classes of graphs, not single actionable hypotheses, and lack reliable, distribution-free uncertainty quantification. This impedes experimental validation in fields like genomics, where high-dimensional data (e.g., transcriptomics) and costly interventions demand precise, confidence-rated predictions.

APPROACH: A two-stage method: (1) Use a scalable constraint-based filter to reduce dimensionality, then apply an end-to-end differentiable model (Gumbel-Softmax adjacency with MLP structural equations) to learn a single graph. (2) Generate edge appearance probabilities via bootstrapping, then calibrate these scores using conformal prediction on benchmark data to produce edge-wise confidence levels with guaranteed false discovery control.

EXPERIMENT: Test on simulated networks and public interventional datasets (e.g., Sachs, Perturb-seq). Measure if calibrated edge confidence (e.g., >0.9) achieves the promised true positive rate (e.g., 90% precision) and outperforms bootstrap/Bayesian baselines in precision-recall on held-out interventional data.

NOVELTY: Integrates differentiable causal discovery with conformal calibration to provide statistically rigorous, edge-level uncertainty guarantees—moving beyond Bayesian or bootstrap heuristics to offer distribution-free confidence for actionable causal hypotheses.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: We propose a conformal prediction wrapper for standard causal discovery algorithms that outputs a sparse causal graph with a finite-sample, statistically valid guarantee on the false discovery rate of edge inclusion, conditional on the algorithm's assumptions.

BACKGROUND: Current causal discovery methods output a single graph or equivalence class without actionable, finite-sample uncertainty quantification for individual edges. This lack of confidence measures severely limits the utility of discovered graphs for prioritizing costly real-world experiments, creating a critical gap between algorithmic output and scientific decision-making.

APPROACH: We will split a full observational dataset into training, calibration, and test sets. Using the calibration set, we will compute a quantile threshold for edge-specific non-conformity scores (e.g., derived from conditional independence test p-values). For a new test dataset, we will run the base algorithm and output a "conformal graph" containing only edges whose scores fall below this threshold, guaranteeing control over the finite-sample selection error of the algorithm.

EXPERIMENT: We will validate the method on public benchmarks (SACHS, LUCAS) and synthetic data from known structural causal models, measuring the empirical false positive rate against ground truth. The core hypothesis will be falsified if this rate systematically exceeds the nominal level (e.g., α=0.05) when the base algorithm's assumptions hold.

NOVELTY: This provides the first finite-sample, assumption-conditional uncertainty guarantees for the graphical output of standard discovery algorithms, transforming them into procedures that output confidence-tagged graphs with a rigorous statistical guarantee on algorithmic uncertainty.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: We propose a hybrid Bayesian-constraint framework that produces causal graphs with calibrated edge-wise uncertainty from mixed-type observational data by explicitly modeling conditional independence test reliability and integrating biomedical knowledge to inform priors on latent confounding.

BACKGROUND: Current causal discovery methods applied to high-dimensional, mixed-type biomedical data (e.g., genomics and EHRs) produce graphs with unreliable confidence estimates. This is because they fail to jointly account for the variable reliability of conditional independence tests across data types and the pervasive, structured nature of latent confounding, creating a critical gap in quantifiably trustworthy causal inference from observational data.

APPROACH: Our method first uses a scalable constraint-based algorithm (FCI) on the full variable set to output a Partial Ancestral Graph, defining a tractable search space and candidate latent confounders. For a focused variable subset, we then apply a Bayesian model whose likelihood scores graph agreement with robust CI test p-values (not binary outcomes) and incorporates a prior over latent confounders informed by UMLS knowledge graph co-mention frequencies.

EXPERIMENT: We will validate on the SACHS network and synthetic benchmarks from `causal-learn`, comparing the calibration (Area Under the Precision-Recall curve for high-probability edges) of our method's posterior probabilities against the PC algorithm and its bootstrapped variant, using a paired t-test across simulation replicates for statistical significance.

NOVELTY: The novelty is the closed-loop integration of a constraint-based skeleton with a focused Bayesian likelihood that treats test p-values as continuous evidence and uses an external knowledge base to structure the prior over latent confounders, enabling data-adaptive, calibrated uncertainty quantification for causal edges.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: This project develops a scalable diagnostic test for latent confounding in high-dimensional causal discovery by introducing a novel metric—the Conditional Dependence Increase (CDI) profile—which quantifies localized violations of Markov constraints from a standard PC run, enabling risk assessment before graph interpretation.

BACKGROUND: Applied causal discovery from high-dimensional observational data (e.g., biobank or EHR studies) critically depends on the causal sufficiency assumption, which is routinely violated by unmeasured common causes. Current latent-variable methods like FCI are computationally intractable at scale, forcing researchers to use insufficient methods like PC and unknowingly accept misleading results; there exists no practical, assumption-light diagnostic to gauge this risk prior to discovery.

APPROACH: The method computes a per-variable score by systematically testing for a specific signature: for many variable triples (X, Y, Z) where X ⫫ Y | Z holds, testing whether X ̸⫫ Y | Z ∪ {W} also holds. A high score for a variable W indicates it systematically induces dependencies, a pattern inconsistent with a faithful, causally sufficient DAG and indicative of W being a child of a latent confounder.

EXPERIMENT: We validate the diagnostic on synthetic DAGs with known injected latent variables, measuring its accuracy (AUC) in classifying confounded variables, and then apply it to produce a ranked list of proteins by latent confounding risk from the observational Sachs signaling data.

NOVELTY: This repurposes foundational graphical model logic into a standalone, pre-discovery diagnostic metric that localizes confounding risk without full latent-variable discovery, bridging the gap between theoretically sound but intractable methods (FCI) and practically used but fragile ones (PC).

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Actively curate a reinforcement learning agent's training distribution by selecting simulator parameters that maximize the reduction of its policy's epistemic uncertainty, thereby achieving superior zero-shot generalization compared to uniform domain randomization for an equivalent computational budget.

BACKGROUND: Uniform Domain Randomization (DR) is a dominant yet sample-inefficient technique for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, operating on the assumption that broader training diversity is always better. This work addresses the open problem of how to strategically, rather than uniformly, sample from a parameterized simulator to construct a training distribution that most efficiently leads to robust generalization.

APPROACH: We pair a standard PPO agent with a meta-controller that, at fixed intervals, selects the next environment parameters from a discrete set. The selection is based on a robust proxy for epistemic uncertainty—specifically, the variance of actions sampled from the agent's stochastic policy across multiple rollouts in candidate environments. The meta-controller uses a Bayesian optimization loop to propose parameters where this policy disagreement is highest, creating an adaptive curriculum.

EXPERIMENT: We will train two agents—one with Active DR and one with Uniform DR—for an identical number of environment steps in a parameterized MuJoCo task (e.g., HalfCheetah). The primary metric is the agents' average zero-shot return on a fixed, held-out test suite of 1000 unseen parameter configurations, with statistical significance tested via a paired t-test.

NOVELTY: This method formalizes and leverages the distinction between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty within the DR paradigm, using policy-level epistemic uncertainty—not task performance or value ensembles—to drive a parameter selection curriculum explicitly designed for generalization.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: We propose a dynamic curriculum for zero-shot RL that first explores via diversity until a novel diversity saturation metric plateaus, then switches to distill skills into a causal representation invariant to nuisance factors, optimizing the trade-off between skill acquisition and robustness.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in RL requires policies robust to unseen nuisance factors (e.g., visual textures). A core open problem is the tension between diversity-driven exploration, which acquires broad skills but is sample-inefficient for learning invariances, and direct invariance learning, which is sample-efficient but can converge to a limited skill set. The optimal integration of these approaches remains an untested, unprincipled engineering challenge.

APPROACH: We formalize this as the Causal Invariance-Diversity Trade-off. Our method trains an agent using a blended objective: a diversity loss (e.g., APS) and an invariance loss (via style-transfer-based contrastive learning). The key innovation is a principled curriculum governed by a Diversity Saturation Metric (DSM), such as the rolling-window entropy of skill embeddings. The diversity loss weight is high initially; when the DSM’s rate of change falls below a threshold, the curriculum automatically reduces the diversity weight and increases the invariance loss weight, shifting focus from skill acquisition to robust distillation.

EXPERIMENT: Using DMControl's Walker-Walk with varied floor textures/colors (nuisances) and morphology (task-relevant), we train three agents (Diversity-First, Invariance-First, and our Dynamic Curriculum) with matched samples. We measure the generalization gap to unseen texture/color combinations and use linear probing to quantify the disentanglement of morphology vs. nuisance factors in the learned representations.

NOVELTY: This introduces a *principled, measurable switching criterion* (the DSM) to dynamically manage the invariance-diversity trade-off, moving beyond fixed schedules or simple combinations to a theory-grounded adaptive curriculum.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: We propose that robustness (via data augmentation) and diversity (via skill discovery) are orthogonal axes of generalization in RL, and we will test the hypothesis that a synergistic agent, combining DrQ and DIAYN objectives on a shared latent representation, achieves superior zero-shot transfer on tasks requiring both robustness to low-level distractors and adaptation to high-level dynamics shifts, without sacrificing sample efficiency.

BACKGROUND: A core open problem in zero-shot RL generalization is the tension between learning robust, invariant representations and learning diverse, adaptable behaviors. Prior work typically optimizes for one axis, but their interaction and potential synergy for tasks with multi-faceted variations remain untested in a controlled, falsifiable manner.

APPROACH: We will train a single agent using SAC with two auxiliary losses on a shared encoder: a DrQ-style invariance loss on augmented pixel views, and a DIAYN-style skill-discrimination loss applied to the encoder's latent representation. This pressures the representation to be both visually invariant and behaviorally informative.

EXPERIMENT: We will train three agents (SAC+DrQ, SAC+DIAYN, SAC+DrQ+DIAYN) on a fixed DMControl task and evaluate zero-shot performance on a 2x2 test suite varying visual distractions and dynamics. The primary metric is the generalization gap to the high-variation condition, supported by skill-consistency metrics and linear probe analysis of the learned representations.

NOVELTY: This work provides the first controlled, mechanistic test of the orthogonality hypothesis, using a diagnostic benchmark to decouple variation axes and a concrete implementation that synergizes objectives at the representation level to achieve complementary generalization benefits.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: We introduce a method that algorithmically certifies and generates a minimal sufficient set of training environments for zero-shot RL generalization by learning a causal proxy model to identify and adversarially sample only reward-causal parameters.

BACKGROUND: Current domain randomization uniformly samples all environment parameters, which is sample-inefficient and can fail catastrophically when nuisance variables (e.g., visual texture) correlate with causal dynamics (e.g., friction). A principled, data-driven method to distinguish and selectively randomize only the minimal set of parameters necessary for generalization remains an open problem.

APPROACH: We train a hypernetwork-based world model on initial exploratory data to compute the sensitivity of predicted dynamics/reward to each environment parameter. Parameters with sensitivity above a threshold are designated causal; we then generate the training distribution by performing MaxEnt or adversarial sampling over only this causal set, holding nuisances nearly constant.

EXPERIMENT: Using DMControl/Isaac Gym tasks with parameterized visual and physical variables, we will measure the generalization gap (performance drop from training to a correlated test set) and sample efficiency of our method against a uniform DR baseline, with statistical significance tested across 5 seeds.

NOVELTY: This provides a formal minimal sufficiency guarantee—the policy is trained only on variations in parameters provably influential to task success—moving beyond uniform sampling or full causal graph discovery to a tractable, certifiable method for generating sufficient training distributions.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: We propose Interventional Domain Randomization (IDR), a framework that online-learns a causal graph of environment parameters and uses it to generate training environments by actively intervening on nuisance variables, thereby systematically breaking spurious correlations with causal factors to enforce robust, zero-shot generalization.

BACKGROUND: Current Domain Randomization (DR) methods uniformly sample environment parameters, an untested assumption that fails when spurious correlations between nuisance (e.g., texture) and causal (e.g., mass) parameters change at test time. This creates a critical gap: a lack of a principled, adaptive methodology for generating training distributions that guarantee generalization by enforcing causal invariance.

APPROACH: IDR periodically estimates parameter influence via performance sensitivity profiling (not gradients) to distinguish causal from nuisance parameters. It then biases the DR sampler to generate environments from an interventional distribution, explicitly minimizing estimated correlations between nuisance and causal parameter pairs, thereby decorrelating them during training.

EXPERIMENT: We will test IDR against uniform DR in a Meta-World `Push` task with a spurious color-mass correlation, measuring the zero-shot success rate differential on a test suite where this correlation is reversed, using identical architectures and fixed training budgets for a controlled comparison.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior adaptive DR methods that optimize for difficulty or coverage, IDR formalizes the data-generating process through online causal graph learning and interventional sampling, directly targeting the removal of spurious correlations for guaranteed invariance.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: This research tests the hypothesis that human-like symbolic properties in emergent communication arise from functional pressure for efficient coordination under strict bandwidth constraints, not from a discrete communication channel, by rigorously decoupling bottleneck severity from channel type and measuring structural alignment between protocols.

BACKGROUND: The field of emergent communication assumes a discrete communication bottleneck is necessary for protocols to develop symbolic properties like categoricality and generalization. This is an untested methodological axiom, as prior work confounds the effects of a strict information constraint with the discreteness of the channel itself, leaving a critical gap in understanding the true causes of symbolism.

APPROACH: We will train agent populations on a referential Lewis Signaling Game with a fixed bandwidth, manipulating only the channel: a discrete one-hot channel, a continuous channel with a matched-dimensionality plus a sparsity penalty, and an unconstrained continuous channel. We will measure symbolic properties via cluster analysis, mutual information, and cross-population generalization, and test for structural alignment using Representational Similarity Analysis between the discrete and bottlenecked-continuous message spaces.

EXPERIMENT: Using ≥5 independent seeds per condition on BabyAI-style tasks, we will compute a composite symbolic property score and compare conditions. A critical falsifying test is a cross-channel transfer experiment, where messages from a discrete-condition sender are translated via an autoencoder to the continuous space; maintained performance with the original receiver confirms the symbolic structure is channel-invariant.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely isolates the causal factor of bandwidth constraint from channel type, predicting and testing for structural alignment between discrete and continuous protocols, thereby refocusing the search for symbolism from architectural mandates to functional pressures.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: We will test the hypothesis that the severity of the cultural transmission bottleneck—operationalized as the number of learning episodes per generation—is a causal driver of compositionality in emergent communication, by systematically varying bottleneck strength within an iterated learning chain of neural agents in a minimal referential game.

BACKGROUND: A key open problem in emergent communication is identifying the precise pressures that cause artificial agents to develop human-like, compositional languages. While cultural evolution via iterated learning is a proposed mechanism, the untested assumption is that bottleneck severity—the limited data available to each new learner—is the critical parameter that creates pressure for compressible, generalizable, and thus compositional protocols.

APPROACH: We will implement a multi-generational iterated learning chain where a frozen sender from one generation trains a naive receiver in a referential game, imposing a controlled bottleneck by limiting the new agent's training episodes. We will directly manipulate bottleneck severity (e.g., 100 vs. 1000 episodes) as the independent variable across parallel chains, and measure the resultant compositional structure.

EXPERIMENT: Using a minimal referential game (3 shapes x 3 colors) with a combinatorial generalization split, we will measure: 1) systematic generalization error on held-out attribute combinations, and 2) Positional Disentanglement (a causal intervention metric quantifying how cleanly single attribute changes affect single message tokens). We will compare iterated chains against a static co-adaptation baseline and a repeated bottleneck control.

NOVELTY: This provides the first direct, causal test of bottleneck severity as the controlling parameter for compositionality in cultural transmission, moving beyond binary "with/without" comparisons to a controlled manipulation of transmission pressure within a dynamic multi-agent system.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: We will provide the first causal mechanistic account of convention formation in emergent communication by demonstrating that stable, shared protocols arise from discrete, identifiable "weight alignment events," where congruent gradient updates from singular cooperative successes lock in specific feature-symbol mappings.

BACKGROUND: Current research in emergent communication can describe *that* a protocol forms and its statistical properties, but it lacks a causal understanding of *how* specific, arbitrary conventions stabilize within the agents' networks. The critical open problem is to move beyond correlation and identify the decisive internal computational steps—the specific network dynamics and weight updates—that are necessary and sufficient for locking in a particular mapping.

APPROACH: We combine gradient trajectory analysis with targeted causal interventions. We first identify convergence points via signal entropy, then use linear probing and activation patching to isolate feature-specific representations. Crucially, we trace these back to pinpoint candidate "alignment episodes"—specific high-reward training steps where gradient cosine similarity between agents spikes. We then test causality by replaying or blocking gradient flow from these episodes in controlled re-trainings.

EXPERIMENT: We train 30+ sender-receiver RNN pairs on a compositional referential game (3x3 attributes). We log gradient norms, cosine similarity, and activations to identify alignment episodes. Causal testing involves: 1) Patching converged sender activations into novel trials to induce symbol flips, and 2) Re-training from pre-alignment checkpoints with clamped gradients from the critical episode, measuring the resultant delay or failure in protocol stabilization.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond descriptive statistics and static network analysis to establish a direct causal link between singular, internal learning events (gradient alignment) and the stabilization of a convention, a mechanistic claim previously unexplored in multi-agent systems.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: This project tests whether a domain-general theory-of-mind prior, acquired through self-supervised inverse dynamics pretraining without communication, scaffolds the emergence of more pragmatic and generalizable communication protocols in multi-agent systems.

BACKGROUND: A core, untested assumption in emergent communication research is the "clean-slate" agent, where language emerges from tabula rasa neural networks. This ignores the pre-existing cognitive biases that scaffold real language evolution. The open problem is to causally test how a structured, socially-relevant inductive bias, isolated from communicative experience, shapes the fundamental properties of an emergent protocol.

APPROACH: We will train populations of agents on a cooperative navigation task with a discrete communication channel, comparing three architectures: monolithic, modular, and a theory-of-mind-primed agent. The critical prior is instilled by pretraining the latter's partner module via a self-supervised inverse dynamics objective on solo agent trajectories, teaching a generic "observation-to-action" mapping before any multi-agent interaction.

EXPERIMENT: We will measure zero-shot cross-population generalization success, the mutual information between messages and the sender's future actions, and alignment via a linear probing classifier. Falsifiable predictions include faster convergence and higher pragmatic content for primed agents, coupled with a measurable initial performance cost due to constrained exploration.

NOVELTY: This provides the first controlled test of how a domain-general social inference prior, divorced from communicative experience, scaffolds communication. The novelty is the specific causal link from passive social-cognitive pretraining to the emergence of pragmatic, interoperable protocols, moving beyond modularity or task-specific pretraining.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: We will test the hypothesis that discrete emergent communication protocols implement aligned, sparse causal circuits across agents by performing targeted activation-steering interventions on sender representations and reciprocal path-patching interventions on receiver circuits to directly control and swap attribute-specific meanings.

BACKGROUND: A core open problem in emergent communication is a lack of causal, mechanistic understanding of how signals function within and between agents. Current research relies on correlational metrics between signals and world states, failing to reveal if internal representations are causally necessary and sufficient for generating and interpreting meaning.

APPROACH: We will train Sender/Receiver pairs on a compositional referential game using EGG. We will identify intervenable feature subspaces for object attributes (e.g., color, shape) in each agent using sparse autoencoders. We will then test causal sufficiency and alignment by patching activations from a source object into a target object's forward pass in the sender and, separately, patching the receiver's early-layer responses to one signal with its responses to another.

EXPERIMENT: We will quantify the causal effect as the systematic, reciprocal bias in the Receiver's action logits following these interventions, with essential controls including null interventions on random features and a non-compositional task baseline to falsify the circuit hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond descriptive correlation by introducing cross-agent causal circuit analysis, using direct intervention to test if specialized internal mechanisms are the necessary and sufficient drivers of coordinated meaning between agents.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: A resource-optimal active learning framework that iteratively steers molecular generation by dynamically selecting both which compounds to synthesize and which assays to run, using a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimizer to efficiently navigate potency-ADMET trade-offs.

BACKGROUND: The hit-to-lead optimization phase requires balancing multiple, often competing, molecular properties under severe constraints of time, cost, and synthetic capacity. Current AI-driven approaches typically treat all experimental data as equally costly or use static assay cascades, failing to optimally allocate a constrained experimental budget across heterogeneous data types of varying fidelity and expense.

APPROACH: The framework integrates a fine-tuned molecular generator with a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimizer. The optimizer models computational predictions and existing experimental data (e.g., IC50, solubility, metabolic stability) as fidelities with associated costs, using a custom acquisition function to jointly select the next batch of 5-10 compounds for synthesis and prescribe a tiered assay plan (e.g., measure solubility only for potent compounds) to maximize Pareto front information gain per unit resource.

EXPERIMENT: Starting from a shared dataset of 50-100 compounds with full experimental data, we will run five iterative design-make-test cycles against three controls (medicinal chemistry design, single-objective REINVENT, a weighted-sum model). Success is defined by a statistically superior hypervolume of the final experimentally-measured Pareto front (IC50, solubility, metabolic stability) after an equal investment of ~150 synthesized compounds.

NOVELTY: This introduces an optimal experimental policy for molecular optimization, where the AI actively manages the assay cascade by dynamically modeling cost, uncertainty, and multi-objective improvement—a synthesis of multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization and generative AI not previously applied to steer real-world drug discovery cycles.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: This research will establish and validate a fully automated, bi-weekly Design-Make-Test-Analyze cycle where a generative AI model, updated with medium-throughput experimental data from its own synthesized proposals, demonstrably outperforms a static model in the real-world optimization of binding affinity and metabolic stability.

BACKGROUND: A critical open problem in AI-driven molecular design is the simulation-to-reality gap, where models trained on historical data fail to generalize to novel, synthesizable compounds with optimized real-world properties. While closed-loop aspiration is common, operationalizing a tightly integrated, automated cycle with concrete experimental proof of iterative improvement remains a significant challenge.

APPROACH: We will implement a controlled, iterative protocol comparing a closed-loop AI model against a static model. Every three weeks, each model will propose 25 novel compounds for a specific kinase target. These will be synthesized via an automated platform, with successful compounds tested in a binding assay (primary feedback) and a microsomal stability assay (lagged feedback). The closed-loop model's predictive oracles will be updated each cycle, and its generator retrained every 2-3 cycles using all accumulated experimental data.

EXPERIMENT: Success is a statistically significant positive trend in the average composite property score (normalized pIC50 & T1/2) over 6 cycles for the closed-loop model, concurrently outperforming the static model in a direct, cycle-by-cycle experimental comparison of synthesized compounds.

NOVELTY: The novelty is the rigorous, controlled demonstration that a high-cadence experimental feedback loop on synthesized molecules—operationalized at a bi-weekly scale—enables an AI to escape its initial data biases and converge on improved multi-property compounds faster than a static model.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: This research introduces empirical resource-aware molecular generation, where a generative model's policy is directly constrained by platform-specific synthesis failure modes learned from real-time robotic feedback, co-optimizing for biological activity and proven synthetic viability.

BACKGROUND: Generative models for molecular design are disconnected from real-world multi-objective optimization because "synthesizability" is approximated by universal computational scores, not a lab's specific capabilities. This leads to proposed molecules that fail synthesis, wasting resources and stalling discovery cycles. The open problem is creating a generative design loop that inherently proposes molecules within the proven capability space of a specific, available synthesis platform.

APPROACH: A GFlowNet, trained to sample from a Pareto frontier of predicted potency and lipophilicity, will have its action space penalized by a learned model of platform-specific failure. This failure model is trained on structured logs from a human-in-the-loop automated flow platform, encoding outcomes (success/failure, crude yield) of attempted syntheses for AI-proposed molecules. The generative policy is updated iteratively to avoid substructures and transformations linked to high failure probability on the specific platform.

EXPERIMENT: Over three cycles, the fine-tuned model's proposals will be compared against a baseline using standard computational filters. The primary metrics are the empirical synthesis success rate and the mean number of planned synthetic steps per molecule, assessed for batches of 24 candidates per cycle while controlling for predicted activity.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond using synthesis data as a post-hoc filter or retraining a generic scorer; instead, it embeds causal, platform-specific chemical constraints directly into the generative policy, fundamentally shifting the search space to the intersection of ideal properties and proven synthetic viability.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: We propose a generative molecular design framework that uses a structured probabilistic graph model to explicitly encode the conditional dependencies and noise profiles of a multi-tiered experimental cascade, enabling closed-loop optimization for the probability of real-world progression rather than a single predicted endpoint.

BACKGROUND: Generative models for drug discovery fail to optimize for actual experimental outcomes because they rely on static, single-fidelity predictors, creating a simulation-to-reality gap. The critical open problem is the inability of these models to leverage the predictive correlations between early, noisy experimental signals (e.g., high-throughput screening) and later, high-fidelity outcomes (e.g., potency, metabolic stability) that define success in lead optimization.

APPROACH: We will implement a 3-cycle closed-loop system where a generative model, fine-tuned via reinforcement learning from a deep multi-fidelity surrogate model, proposes compounds. Each cycle integrates real, tiered feedback: high-throughput biochemical screening (% inhibition) for all compounds, followed by confirmatory dose-response/SPR and rapid microsomal stability assays for top performers. The surrogate is a graph neural network explicitly trained to model the conditional probability of success at each experimental tier.

EXPERIMENT: Over 6-9 months, we will test the system on a novel kinase target, synthesizing 10-20 novel compounds per cycle and supplementing with commercially available analogs. The primary metric is a statistically significant increase in hit rate (IC50 < 1 µM) in later cycles versus both the first cycle and a control model optimized only for a pre-trained QSAR-predicted IC50.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond standard multi-feedback loops by using a structured probabilistic model of the experimental cascade itself as the optimization objective, shifting the goal from predicting a single property to maximizing the likelihood of surviving real-world attrition.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: This research will test the hypothesis that a generative AI loop, using a disease-relevant cellular phenotype assay as its primary optimization target and integrated metabolic stability data as a secondary constraint, produces small molecules with superior in vivo pharmacokinetics compared to standard affinity-first design.

BACKGROUND: Current generative models for drug discovery fail because they optimize for simple, poor proxies of success like binding affinity, neglecting the multi-parameter reality of costly, slow-to-measure properties like functional cellular activity and metabolic stability. This creates a critical gap between computationally designed molecules and those that succeed in vivo.

APPROACH: We will establish a closed-loop between a 3D molecule generator and real-world assays. A 3D diffusion model, initially trained on public structure-activity data, will propose 20-30 synthetically accessible compounds per cycle. These will be synthesized and tested in parallel in a functional cellular efficacy assay (e.g., pathway rescue) and a microsomal stability assay. A separate predictive model, updated each cycle, will rank proposals using this combined data to select compounds for the next iteration.

EXPERIMENT: After 4-5 cycles, the top 5-10 molecules from this loop will be compared in a rodent PK study against 3-5 molecules from a state-of-the-art baseline model optimized only for affinity. The primary metric is a statistically significant improvement in plasma exposure (AUC). Failure to show this improvement falsifies the core hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work shifts the primary generative objective from binding to integrated functional cellular efficacy and stability, a deliberate experimental design choice not yet rigorously tested. The novelty is the causal claim that this specific feedback loop provides a more predictive surrogate for in vivo success than affinity-based optimization.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: To collapse the dominant analog-digital interface energy in neuromorphic cores, we propose a co-designed analog-digital hierarchy where an event-driven analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is conditionally triggered by the activity of a digital weight sub-network, governed by an adaptive feedback loop that tunes analog precision based on real-time digital confidence.

BACKGROUND: The "Analog-Digital Chasm"—the energy cost of converting analog crossbar outputs to digital signals—often dominates neuromorphic system energy, rendering low-energy synaptic operations moot. Current hybrid precision or event-driven schemes are static, lacking the tight, input-dependent co-design needed to dynamically minimize this interface overhead without sacrificing robustness.

APPROACH: We implement a hybrid-precision core where most-significant weight bits are in digital SRAM and least-significant bits in analog RRAM. Critically, a digital computation gatekeeps a high-precision ADC: only when the digital contribution exceeds a dynamic threshold is the ADC activated. This threshold is adaptively tuned by a feedback loop that adjusts the analog read voltage based on recent ADC trigger rate, optimizing the precision-energy trade-off per input.

EXPERIMENT: We validate via a three-stage protocol: 1) Algorithmic modeling in Lava/Nengo on N-MNIST to verify >95% of a fixed-precision baseline accuracy; 2) FPGA emulation with injected RRAM variability to measure system-level energy reduction and ADC inactivity (>80%); 3) Fabrication of a minimal 65nm test chip (32x4 column + ADC) to physically measure interface energy and validate thermal robustness (±20°C).

NOVELTY: The novelty is the adaptive, conditional triggering of the ADC by the digital sub-network, creating a dynamic feedback loop between digital activity and analog precision—a tightly coupled co-design that moves beyond static hybrid schemes to actively minimize conversion energy in real-time.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
**IDEA:** We propose a neuromorphic crossbar architecture where a single memristive material, operated in two distinct regimes, creates functionally heterogeneous synapses that, combined with a simplified local learning rule, harness intrinsic device stochasticity for energy-efficient, on-chip temporal credit assignment.

**BACKGROUND:** Temporal credit assignment in spiking neural networks remains a major challenge for on-chip learning, typically requiring complex, energy-expensive digital circuits. Simultaneously, the inherent stochasticity and variability of emerging memristive synapses are often treated as a nuisance to be suppressed, rather than a computational resource.

**APPROACH:** We will fabricate a 128x128 1T1R crossbar using a uniform HfO₂ synaptic stack.
